claim: Adult male cats weighing 2.5–3.5 kg were used in the experiments.
source: Adult male cats (2.5–3.5 kg) were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of Nembutal (25 mg/kg), and paralyzed with gallamine triethiodide (Flaxedil) and artificially ventilated (end tidal CO2 held at 4.0%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Anesthesia was maintained by continuous infusion of sodium thiopental (3–10 mg/kg/h) for some experiments (n = 40).
source: Anesthesia was maintained by continuous infusion of sodium thiopental (3–10 mg/kg/h) for some experiments (n = 40), and propofol (3–4 mg/kg/hr) for others (n = 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in a specific number of experiments.

claim: Anesthesia was maintained by continuous infusion of propofol (3–4 mg/kg/hr) for some experiments (n = 4).

claim: A desynchronized pattern of EEG without predominant slow oscillations, but with occasional spindles, was maintained throughout the experiment.

evidence: This describes the physiological state maintained during experiments, with citation to support the characterization.

claim: L4 simple cells were consistently found between 500 and 950 um depth.
source: L4 simple cells were consistently found between 500 and 950 um, as measured from the micropositioner.
evidence: This is a direct observation about the anatomical location of recorded cells.

claim: Recordings were digitized at 33 KHz and downsampled to 10 KHz.
source: Recordings were digitized at 33 KHz (Neuralynx) and downsampled to 10 KHz.
evidence: This describes the technical parameters of data acquisition.

claim: All cortical cells used in this study had a stable Vm below −60 mV, without holding current, had overshooting action potentials, and were observed for at least 10 min.
source: All cortical cells used in this study had a stable Vm below −60 mV, without holding current, had overshooting action potentials, and were observed for at least 10 min.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for cells in the study.

claim: The study recorded from 28 cells in L4 of V1.
source: To study the dynamic properties of thalamocortical synapses in vivo, we recorded simultaneously from the LGN and its postsynaptic targets in L4 (n = 28) or L6 (n = 8) of V1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of cells recorded in a specific layer.

claim: The study recorded from 8 cells in L6 of V1.
source: To study the dynamic properties of thalamocortical synapses in vivo, we recorded simultaneously from the LGN and its postsynaptic targets in L4 (n = 28) or L6 (n = 8) of V1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of cells recorded in a specific layer.

claim: All cortical cells in the database were simple cells since no connections with complex cells were found.
source: All cortical cells in the database were simple cells since we found no connections with complex cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cell types included in the study.

claim: No differences were found between simple cells in L4 and those in L6.
source: Furthermore, we found no differences between simple cells in L4 with those in L6 and therefore the data are presented together.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison between cell populations.

claim: Spikes from 4 to 25 LGN neurons were recorded extracellularly with independently movable tetrodes.
source: Spikes from 4 to 25 LGN neurons were recorded extracellularly with independently movable tetrodes, while the membrane potential (Vm) of V1 neurons was recorded with intracellular sharp electrodes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and number of neurons recorded.

claim: The membrane potential (Vm) of V1 neurons was recorded with intracellular sharp electrodes.
source: Spikes from 4 to 25 LGN neurons were recorded extracellularly with independently movable tetrodes, while the membrane potential (Vm) of V1 neurons was recorded with intracellular sharp electrodes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the recording technique used for V1 neurons.

claim: 36 LGN cells were found to be monosynaptically connected to 23 cortical simple cells.
source: Using this procedure, we found 36 LGN cells monosynaptically connected to 23 cortical simple cells, from a total of 296 simultaneously recorded pairs with overlapping receptive fields.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of connected pairs identified.

claim: 296 LGN-V1 pairs with overlapping receptive fields were simultaneously recorded.
source: Using this procedure, we found 36 LGN cells monosynaptically connected to 23 cortical simple cells, from a total of 296 simultaneously recorded pairs with overlapping receptive fields.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the total number of pairs recorded.

claim: The average EPSP amplitude ranged from 0.15 to 1.2 mV, with a mean of 0.42 mV.
source: Since our previous report with this same dataset (Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017) showed surprisingly small average EPSPs (from 0.15 to 1.2 mV, mean = 0.42 mV), here we aimed to understand the dynamics of the EPSPs triggered by single LGN spikes (single-spike EPSPs) that contribute to the average.
evidence: This cites a previous publication reporting measured EPSP amplitudes from the same dataset.

claim: The mean percent of undetectable EPSPs for the population was 37 ± 12%.
source: The mean percent of undetectable EPSPs for the population (n = 36 pairs) was 37 ± 12% [mean ± SD], ranging from 7.4% to 56% (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter across the population.

claim: The percent of undetectable EPSPs ranged from 7.4% to 56%.
source: The mean percent of undetectable EPSPs for the population (n = 36 pairs) was 37 ± 12% [mean ± SD], ranging from 7.4% to 56% (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the range of a measured parameter.

claim: The average EPSP amplitude was 0.49 ± 0.23 mV when including all single-spike traces.
source: Across the population of connected pairs, the average EPSP amplitude was 0.49 ± 0.23 mV when including all single-spike traces (Figure 4B, black), and significantly higher at 0.89 ± 0.24 mV (p=3e-9, Figure 4D, 'A' vs. 'D') when considering only detectable EPSPs (Figure 4B, green).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter with statistical information.

claim: The average EPSP amplitude was 0.89 ± 0.24 mV when considering only detectable EPSPs.
source: Across the population of connected pairs, the average EPSP amplitude was 0.49 ± 0.23 mV when including all single-spike traces (Figure 4B, black), and significantly higher at 0.89 ± 0.24 mV (p=3e-9, Figure 4D, 'A' vs. 'D') when considering only detectable EPSPs (Figure 4B, green).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter with statistical information.

claim: The average EPSP amplitude for detectable EPSPs is significantly higher than for all spikes (p=3e-9).
source: Across the population of connected pairs, the average EPSP amplitude was 0.49 ± 0.23 mV when including all single-spike traces (Figure 4B, black), and significantly higher at 0.89 ± 0.24 mV (p=3e-9, Figure 4D, 'A' vs. 'D') when considering only detectable EPSPs (Figure 4B, green).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison.

claim: The population average amplitude for jittered spikes was 0.01 ± 0.03 mV.
source: The population average amplitude for jittered spikes was close to 0 (0.01 ± 0.03) mV as expected.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured control parameter.

claim: The population average for undetectable EPSPs was −0.20 ± 0.09 mV, significantly different from 0 (p=5e-15).
source: In contrast, the population average for undetectable EPSPs was −0.20 ± 0.09 mV, significantly different from 0 (p=5e-15 Figure 4D, 'U').
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter with statistical significance.

claim: The mean CV across the population was 1.2 ± 0.47.
source: In agreement with the large variability displayed by the traces in Figure 2B, we found large values of CV across the population, with a mean of 1.2 ± 0.47 (Figure 4C, black).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter.

claim: The mean CV was nearly an order of magnitude larger than reports from in vitro studies of the cat thalamocortical pathway.
source: This is nearly an order of magnitude larger than reports from in vitro studies of the cat thalamocortical pathway (Stratford et al., 1996) and is consistent with the high fraction of undetectable EPSPs.
evidence: This compares the measured CV to previously published values.

claim: After removing undetectable EPSPs, the mean CV reduced to 0.18 ± 0.13.
source: Indeed, the CV distribution shifted towards much lower values after removing undetectable EPSPs and its mean reduced tenfold (0.18 ± 0.13, Figure 4C, green), indicating that much of the variability could be explained by undetectable EPSPs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter after data filtering.

claim: The percentage of undetectable EPSPs was negatively correlated with the average EPSP amplitude (r = −0.81).
source: Across the population, the percentage of undetectable EPSPs was negatively correlated with the average EPSP amplitude (r = −0.81; Figure 4E, left).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the percentage of undetectable EPSPs and CV (r = 0.77).
source: In addition, we observed a positive correlation between the percentage of undetectable EPSPs and CV (r = 0.77; Figure 4E, right), consistent with previous reports in vitro.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result with reference to prior work.

claim: The correlation between CV and average EPSP amplitude remained after exclusion of undetectable EPSPs (r = −0.66).
source: The exclusion of undetectable EPSPs did not change the correlation between CV and average EPSP amplitude (Figure 4F, right; r = −0.66), indicating that these two values are negatively correlated independent of detectability.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result after data filtering.

claim: 16 out of 23 cortical cells were classified as regular-spiking (RS).
source: To determine if synaptic reliability or variability were related with the electrophysiological class of the target V1 cell, we classified our L4 simple cells into regular-spiking (RS; n = 16/23) and fast-spiking (FS; n = 7/23) based on their intracellularly measured electrophysiological properties (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cell classification.

claim: 7 out of 23 cortical cells were classified as fast-spiking (FS).
source: To determine if synaptic reliability or variability were related with the electrophysiological class of the target V1 cell, we classified our L4 simple cells into regular-spiking (RS; n = 16/23) and fast-spiking (FS; n = 7/23) based on their intracellularly measured electrophysiological properties (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cell classification.

claim: 24 presynaptic LGN cells were connected to RS cortical cells.
source: Of the 36 presynaptic LGN cells, 24 were connected to RS cortical cells (Figure 4, blue dots) and 12 were connected to FS cells (Figure 4, red dots).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of connections.

claim: 12 presynaptic LGN cells were connected to FS cortical cells.
source: Of the 36 presynaptic LGN cells, 24 were connected to RS cortical cells (Figure 4, blue dots) and 12 were connected to FS cells (Figure 4, red dots).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of connections.

claim: No significant difference was found in average EPSP amplitude, %undetectable, or CV between RS and FS cells.
source: We did not find a significant difference in either average EPSP amplitude, %undetectable, or CV between RS and FS cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a statistical comparison.

claim: After excluding undetectable EPSP traces, the mean CV of RS cells (0.22 ± 0.13) was higher than that of FS cells (0.11 ± 0.08; p=0.047 KS test, p=0.018 t-test).
source: However, after excluding undetectable EPSP traces, the mean CV of RS cells (n = 24, 0.22 ± 0.13) was higher than that of FS cells (n = 12, 0.11 ± 0.08; p=0.047 KS test, p=0.018 t-test; Figure 4D) and the average EPSP amplitude (Figure 4F, x-axis) was smaller for RS (0.83 ± 0.21 mV) than for FS cells (1.0 ± 0.21 mV; p=0.0046 KStest, p=0.025 t-test; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison result.

claim: After excluding undetectable EPSPs, the average EPSP amplitude was smaller for RS cells (0.83 ± 0.21 mV) than for FS cells (1.0 ± 0.21 mV; p=0.0046 KStest, p=0.025 t-test).
source: However, after excluding undetectable EPSP traces, the mean CV of RS cells (n = 24, 0.22 ± 0.13) was higher than that of FS cells (n = 12, 0.11 ± 0.08; p=0.047 KS test, p=0.018 t-test; Figure 4D) and the average EPSP amplitude (Figure 4F, x-axis) was smaller for RS (0.83 ± 0.21 mV) than for FS cells (1.0 ± 0.21 mV; p=0.0046 KStest, p=0.025 t-test; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison result.

claim: The average slope of single-spike EPSPs was slightly higher for FS cells (1.14 ± 0.23) compared to RS cells (0.97 ± 0.18) (p=0.023 KStest; p=0.027 t-test), only after excluding undetectable EPSPs.
source: Similarly, the average slope of single-spike EPSPs was slightly higher for FS cells (1.14 ± 0.23) compared to RS cells (0.97 ± 0.18) (p=0.023 KStest; p=0.027 t-test), only after excluding undetectable EPSPs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison result.

claim: Five cortical cells had three connected LGN cells each.
source: Our dataset included five cortical cells with three connected LGN cells each (Figure 4G, red dots) and three cortical cells with two connected LGN cells each (Figure 4G, green dots), the remaining 15 cortical cells had a single connected LGN cell (Figure 4G, black dots).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset composition.

claim: Three cortical cells had two connected LGN cells each.
source: Our dataset included five cortical cells with three connected LGN cells each (Figure 4G, red dots) and three cortical cells with two connected LGN cells each (Figure 4G, green dots), the remaining 15 cortical cells had a single connected LGN cell (Figure 4G, black dots).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset composition.

claim: 15 cortical cells had a single connected LGN cell.
source: Our dataset included five cortical cells with three connected LGN cells each (Figure 4G, red dots) and three cortical cells with two connected LGN cells each (Figure 4G, green dots), the remaining 15 cortical cells had a single connected LGN cell (Figure 4G, black dots).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset composition.

claim: The CV of connections to the same postsynaptic V1 cell was as variable as that of connections across different cortical cells.
source: We plotted the CV of all connections in rank order and found that the CV of connections to the same postsynaptic V1 cell was as variable as that of connections across different cortical cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis of CV variability.

claim: The postsynaptic cell does not overtly determine the variability of LGN-V1 synapses.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the postsynaptic cell does not overtly determine the variability of LGN-V1 synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of CV variability across connections.

claim: A subset (n = 19) of connected pairs were tested during the response to oriented drifting grating stimuli.
source: Finally, to verify that synaptic properties were not dependent on the type of visual stimulus presented, we separately calculated amplitude distributions and %undetectable for a subset (n = 19) of connected pairs during the response to oriented drifting grating stimuli (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a subset of the data analyzed under different conditions.

claim: There was a high correlation between the average EPSP amplitude during white noise and gratings (r = 0.90).
source: We found a high correlation between the average EPSP amplitude during the response to both white noise and gratings (Figure 4H, left, r = 0.90), as well as between the standard deviation of the amplitude distribution (r = 0.85, data not shown), and between %undetectable (Figure 4H, right, r = 0.82).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result.

claim: There was a high correlation between the standard deviation of the amplitude distribution during white noise and gratings (r = 0.85).
source: We found a high correlation between the average EPSP amplitude during the response to both white noise and gratings (Figure 4H, left, r = 0.90), as well as between the standard deviation of the amplitude distribution (r = 0.85, data not shown), and between %undetectable (Figure 4H, right, r = 0.82).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result.

claim: There was a high correlation between %undetectable during white noise and gratings (r = 0.82).
source: We found a high correlation between the average EPSP amplitude during the response to both white noise and gratings (Figure 4H, left, r = 0.90), as well as between the standard deviation of the amplitude distribution (r = 0.85, data not shown), and between %undetectable (Figure 4H, right, r = 0.82).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result.

claim: The average EPSP amplitude was significantly higher during white noise stimuli (p=0.0055).
source: We found that the average EPSP amplitude was significantly higher during white noise stimuli (p=0.0055), but all other variables including LGN firing rate had similar distributions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison result.

claim: 20 out of 36 connected pairs (55%) exhibited significant STSP.
source: Using this metric, we found that 20 out of our population of 36 connected pairs (55%) exhibited significant STSP.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the prevalence of short-term synaptic plasticity.

claim: Of the 20 connected pairs that exhibited STSP, 17 exhibited STSD and three exhibited STSF.
source: Of the 20 connected pairs that exhibited STSP (Figure 5E, both +amp bars), 17 exhibited STSD and three exhibited STSF.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the types of plasticity observed.

claim: The %change across the 17 connected pairs exhibiting STSD was −32 ± 15%.
source: The %change across the 17 connected pairs exhibiting STSD was −32 ± 15%, and the %change across the three connected pairs exhibiting STSF was 24 ± 16%.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter.

claim: The %change across the three connected pairs exhibiting STSF was 24 ± 16%.
source: The %change across the 17 connected pairs exhibiting STSD was −32 ± 15%, and the %change across the three connected pairs exhibiting STSF was 24 ± 16%.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured parameter.

claim: All three synapses exhibiting significant STSF were connected onto FS cortical cells.
source: Notably, all three synapses exhibiting significant STSF were connected onto FS cortical cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cell type specificity of a phenomenon.

claim: RS cells only exhibited significant STSD.
source: RS cells only exhibited significant STSD.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cell type specificity of a phenomenon.

claim: Most (14/20) connected pairs that exhibited distinct EPSP amplitude distributions for short and long ISIs also exhibited distinct ISI distributions for detectable and undetectable single-spike EPSPs.
source: Across the population, most (14/20) connected pairs that exhibited distinct EPSP amplitude distributions for short and long ISIs also exhibited distinct ISI distributions for detectable and undetectable single-spike EPSPs (Figure 5E, 'both').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relationship between two measured phenomena.

claim: Connected pairs with larger average EPSP amplitudes undergo greater STSD.
source: Consistent with such models, we found that the connected pairs with larger average EPSP amplitudes undergo greater STSD (Figure 5G, left), and those with smaller average EPSPs undergo STSF (%change >0; Figure 5G, left).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relationship between EPSP amplitude and plasticity.

claim: Connected pairs with smaller average EPSPs undergo STSF.
source: Consistent with such models, we found that the connected pairs with larger average EPSP amplitudes undergo greater STSD (Figure 5G, left), and those with smaller average EPSPs undergo STSF (%change >0; Figure 5G, left).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relationship between EPSP amplitude and plasticity.

claim: There was a small positive correlation between the CV and %change.
source: Furthermore, we also found a small positive correlation between the CV and %change (Figure 5G, right), with synapses with larger CVs exhibiting smaller STSD.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a correlation analysis result.

claim: No correlation was found between the amount of STSP in a connected pair and the firing rate of the pre-synaptic LGN cell within a range of 2–24 Hz.
source: Finally, we did not find a correlation between the amount of STSP in a connected pair and the firing rate of the pre-synaptic LGN cell within a range of 2–24 Hz (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of correlation between two variables.

claim: Thalamocortical synapses exhibit STSP, with FS cells exhibiting STSD and STSF equally and RS cells exhibiting only STSD.
source: All together, we conclude that a) thalamocortical synapses exhibit STSP, with FS cells exhibiting STSD and STSF equally and RS cells exhibiting only STSD; b) at the single synapse level, spiking history influences the detectability of the EPSP and thus the influence on postsynaptic spike output; c) STSD in vivo is independent of pre-synaptic firing rate, and is associated with EPSP amplitude reductions of ~30%.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: At the single synapse level, spiking history influences the detectability of the EPSP and thus the influence on postsynaptic spike output.
source: All together, we conclude that a) thalamocortical synapses exhibit STSP, with FS cells exhibiting STSD and STSF equally and RS cells exhibiting only STSD; b) at the single synapse level, spiking history influences the detectability of the EPSP and thus the influence on postsynaptic spike output; c) STSD in vivo is independent of pre-synaptic firing rate, and is associated with EPSP amplitude reductions of ~30%.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: STSD in vivo is independent of pre-synaptic firing rate, and is associated with EPSP amplitude reductions of ~30%.
source: All together, we conclude that a) thalamocortical synapses exhibit STSP, with FS cells exhibiting STSD and STSF equally and RS cells exhibiting only STSD; b) at the single synapse level, spiking history influences the detectability of the EPSP and thus the influence on postsynaptic spike output; c) STSD in vivo is independent of pre-synaptic firing rate, and is associated with EPSP amplitude reductions of ~30%.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Variable and unreliable synapses increase cortical firing by means of increasing membrane fluctuations, similar to high conductance states.
source: Using biologically constrained models, we found that variable and unreliable synapses serve to increase cortical firing by means of increasing membrane fluctuations, similar to high conductance states.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling based on experimental data.

claim: The V1 cell with unreliable synapses fired action potentials, while the cell with reliable synapses did not, due to the presence of larger fluctuations in its input current.
source: In this example, only the V1 cell with unreliable synapses fired action potentials, due to the presence of larger fluctuations in its Iin.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the model simulation.

claim: For a V1 cell driven by 50 LGN neurons with unreliable synapses, the average V1 firing rate was 7.8 ± 1.4 spikes/sec.
source: For a V1 cell driven by 50 LGN neurons with unreliable synapses, the average V1 firing rate was 7.8 ± 1.4 spikes/sec whereas for reliable synapses it was 1.8 ± 0.84 spikes/sec.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model output.

claim: For a V1 cell driven by 50 LGN neurons with reliable synapses, the average V1 firing rate was 1.8 ± 0.84 spikes/sec.
source: For a V1 cell driven by 50 LGN neurons with unreliable synapses, the average V1 firing rate was 7.8 ± 1.4 spikes/sec whereas for reliable synapses it was 1.8 ± 0.84 spikes/sec.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model output.

claim: Vm SD, and not mean Vm, determines cortical firing rate for both reliable and unreliable synapses.
source: In addition, this relationship demonstrates that Vm SD, and not mean Vm, determines cortical firing rate for both reliable and unreliable synapses (Figure 7D, right).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: The effect of EPSP variability is larger than the effect of failure rate on increased cortical firing rate in the unreliable model.
source: We found that the effect of EPSP variability is larger than the effect of failure rate, although we recognize that EPSP variability and reliability are not independent in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion from a control simulation comparing different model variants.

claim: The unreliable model with correlated failures still produced higher cortical VmSD and firing.
source: We found that the unreliable model with correlated failures (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, blue traces) still produced higher cortical VmSD and firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion from a control simulation with a different failure distribution.

claim: Thalamocortical synapses in vivo are weak and unreliable.
source: We found that thalamocortical synapses are highly variable and unreliable, and exhibit short-term plasticity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Thalamocortical synapses exhibit short-term plasticity.
source: We found that thalamocortical synapses are highly variable and unreliable, and exhibit short-term plasticity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Synaptic variability and unreliability, rather than acting as system noise, do serve a computational function.
source: Thus, synaptic variability and unreliability, rather than acting as system noise, do serve a computational function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Thalamocortical connections had large amplitudes (~2 mV) with little variability (CV ~0.1) in slices of the cat thalamocortical pathway.
source: This differs drastically from findings in slices of the cat thalamocortical pathway (Stratford et al., 1996; Bannister et al., 2002), which indicated that thalamocortical connections had large amplitudes (~2 mV) with little variability (CV ~0.1).
evidence: This cites previous in vitro studies for comparison with the current in vivo results.

claim: The EPSP amplitudes measured in vivo (~0.9 mV, mean including only detectable) are comparable to in vivo measurements of thalamocortical EPSP amplitude in the rodent L4 barrel cortex.
source: However, the EPSP amplitudes that we measured (~0.9 mV, mean including only detectable) are comparable to in vivo measurements of thalamocortical EPSP amplitude in the rodent L4 barrel cortex calculated by either STA from simultaneously recorded VB spikes (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006); 0.9 mV) or from minimal electrical stimulation in the white matter(Schoonover et al., 2014); 1.0 mV).
evidence: This compares the measured values to previously published in vivo measurements in a different system.

claim: The average %undetectable rate of ~40% is double the value reported from in vivo single-cell stimulation studies in mouse L2/3 excitatory intracortical connections.
source: There are no published reports of in vivo thalamocortical synaptic failure rates for comparison, but our average %undetectable rate of ~40% is double the value reported from in vivo single-cell stimulation studies in mouse L2/3 excitatory intracortical connections (Jouhanneau et al., 2015).
evidence: This compares the measured failure rate to a published value from a different circuit.

claim: Boudreau and Ferster (2005) found depression rates of 20% for electrical stimulation of the LGN at 20 Hz, and of 40% for the highest stimulation rate of 100 Hz.
source: This is consistent with previous reports of synaptic depression in the thalamocortical pathway of the anesthetized cat carried out by Boudreau and Ferster (2005). They found depression rates of 20% for electrical stimulation of the LGN at 20 Hz, and of 40% for the highest stimulation rate of 100 Hz.
evidence: This cites a previous study for comparison with the current findings on synaptic depression.

claim: LGN cells from the lateral geniculate nucleus respond to visual input with temporally precise spikes.
source: In the visual system, thalamic cells from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) respond to visual input with temporally precise spikes (Reinagel and Reid, 2000; Liu et al., 2001; Kumbhani et al., 2007).
evidence: This cites previous studies characterizing LGN response properties.

claim: No more than 10% of the synapses onto thalamorecipient cortical cells in V1 are of thalamic origin.
source: In addition, it has become clear that no more than 10% of the synapses onto thalamorecipient cortical cells in V1 are of thalamic origin (Ahmed et al., 1998; Peters and Payne, 1993; da Costa and Martin, 2009).
evidence: This cites anatomical studies about the proportion of thalamic synapses.

claim: Experimental data indicate that thalamic input accounts for 1/2 to 1/3 of the activity in L4.
source: However, experimental data indicate that thalamic input accounts for 1/2 to 1/3 of the activity in L4 (Chung and Ferster, 1998).
evidence: This cites a previous study about the contribution of thalamic input to cortical activity.

claim: A seminal in vitro study reported powerful and invariant thalamocortical synapses in the cat.
source: A seminal in vitro study (Stratford et al., 1996) reported powerful and invariant thalamocortical synapses in the cat, suggesting that it is the relative strength of these synapses, compared to the more numerous intracortical synapses, that contributes to the disproportionate effect of the thalamus on V1.
evidence: This cites a previous in vitro study for comparison with the current findings.

claim: The findings are consistent with recent work suggesting synaptic variability and reliability play an important role in ethologically relevant behaviors.
source: Our findings are consistent with recent work suggesting synaptic variability and reliability play an important role in ethologically relevant behaviors (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites a recent study to contextualize the current findings.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous work in vivo showing different input resistance and membrane time-constant for RS and FS cells.
source: This is consistent with previous work from our laboratory in vivo, showing different input resistance and membrane time-constant for RS and FS cells (Contreras and Palmer, 2003; Cardin et al., 2007; Cardin et al., 2010), and consistent with greater differences observed in vitro across these cell types (Hull et al., 2009; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Schiff and Reyes, 2012; Kloc and Maffei, 2014).
evidence: This cites previous studies from the same laboratory and others for comparison.

claim: The findings are consistent with greater differences observed in vitro across RS and FS cell types.
source: This is consistent with previous work from our laboratory in vivo, showing different input resistance and membrane time-constant for RS and FS cells (Contreras and Palmer, 2003; Cardin et al., 2007; Cardin et al., 2010), and consistent with greater differences observed in vitro across these cell types (Hull et al., 2009; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Schiff and Reyes, 2012; Kloc and Maffei, 2014).

claim: An inverse relationship between the rate of spike-transmission failures and average EPSP amplitude has been previously reported in a variety of circuits both in vitro and in vivo.
